newsitem.title: TURKEY: Turkey seeks reassurance EU not a Christian club.
newsitem.headline: Turkey seeks reassurance EU not a Christian club.

text.p: Turkey sought reassurance on Wednesday that its Moslem identity would not block entry into the European Union after the issue of its religious make-up was raised by a senior EU official.

"We were openly told the EU is not a Christian club. We want to believe that these statements of the EU's high-ranking officials were sincere," Turkish Foreign Ministry spokesman Omer Akbel told a news conference.

Akbel was speaking in response to comments by Dutch Foreign Minister Hans van Mierlo who said on Tuesday Europe faced difficulties in fully embracing Turkey, ranging from its human rights record to its religious identity.
"There is a problem of a large Moslem state. Do we want that in Europe? It is an unspoken question," van Mierlo told a European Parliament committee on behalf of the Dutch EU presidency.
Ninety-nine percent Moslem but secular Turkey signed an association agreement with what is now the European Union as long ago as 1963 and formally applied to join the bloc in 1987.
The European Commission, which vets countries' membership applications, ruled that Turkey was not ready on both economic and democratic grounds.
Formal negotiations with as many as 11 candidate countries -- but not Turkey -- are due to start around the end of this year.
The EU's "Big Five" powers -- Britain, France, Germany, Italy and Spain -- met Turkish Foreign Minister Tansu Ciller in Rome last week to talk over relations between Ankara and the EU.
They said there were "no obstacles in principle" to Turkey's future membership. Western officials are keen to avoid having Turkey's Islamist-led government turn its back on Europe.
Turkey's relations with the EU are complicated by Ankara's long-standing rivalry with Greece, which has blocked EU aid to Turkey.

Ciller has said Ankara could block NATO expansion into Eastern Europe if it was not allowed to join the EU. NATO Secretary-General Javier Solana, due to arrive in Turkey on Wednesday for an official visit, said during a stopover in Hungary that he did not expect Ankara to block the expansion.
